thread.title: McKee pauses Flock cameras; Campbell defends technology
thread.title_full: McKee pauses Flock cameras; Campbell defends technology

author: ohtadmin
title: McKee pauses Flock cameras; Campbell defends technology
text:
Gov. Dan McKee paused new installations of Flock cameras on state property Tuesday less than 12 hours after the town council discussed the controversial technology at its meeting Monday.
Flock cameras, or automated license plate readers, have been criticized by the American Civil Liberty Union as being “Big Brother” surveillance. There also have been reports across the nation about police officers abusing the system by stalking ex-partners using the data.
“Automated license plate readers can be an important tool for law enforcement to solve crimes, recover stolen vehicles and locate dangerous or missing individuals, but Rhode Islanders also have legitimate questions about privacy, transparency and how this information is collected, stored and shared,” McKee said. “Public safety and personal privacy are not mutually exclusive. Rhode Island needs clear and consistent rules of the road for this technology. We are taking action now to pause further expansion, examine how these systems are being used across the state, and put strong, uniform safeguards in place to protect both public safety and personal privacy.”
Councilwoman Mary Meagher requested the discussion at Monday’s meeting to clarify misconceptions about the Flock camera in Jamestown. The camera was installed by state police at the eastern end of the Verrazzano Bridge.
“It’s not my intent to bring this up as an issue,” she said. “It’s more to give information to the community.”
The state police, according to Town Administrator Ed Mello, contacted the chief of police, Jamie Campbell, “almost a year ago … looking for approval” to install the camera. Because the site of the proposed camera was on a state-owned right-of-way on a state-owned road, the request for approval was “a courtesy,” as permission from the town was not needed.
Mello, who served as chief of police from 2011-23, however, endorsed the camera, whose data cannot be accessed by local authorities.
“I directed the chief to send a letter back to the state police to say we had no objection to that,” he said. “Keep in mind, at that time, we were in different place with Flock cameras … The context at the time was that Flock didn’t have the negative attention that it has today. I viewed it as the same technology they are using for all their cameras, their tolling systems, their Bluetooth technology. I did not see it as anything different than that. Clearly the Flock camera, as far as public concern, has evolved since then.”
Campbell, while recognizing the reported misuse of the technology, indicated support.
“My job is to protect citizens, save lives and solve crimes,” he said. “That’s the oath I took. This is what we try to do every day.”
Flock cameras, Campbell said, can help him do that job. A suicidal person who drove through Jamestown to jump off the Pell Bridge, for example, was identified and rescued using data collected from the camera.
“We have seen them locate kidnapped children in this state,” Campbell said. “Track down dementia patients. If your loved one takes the vehicle for a ride, and you call the police and you’re standing at your door in tears panicking because we can’t find somebody? This is what these devices are designed to do. We turn to Flock when we need it. People don’t want Flock cameras, but I’m telling you right now, when something happens, this is a tool that can help save a life, solve a crime and protect the citizens of Jamestown.”
The council’s vice president, Erik Brine, asked Campbell if he’s approached the state police for information gathered by its Flock camera. The chief referenced a financial crime last week.
“I was prepared,” he replied. “I was very close to calling the state police to ask for assistance with a Flock camera. But the investigation took a different direction, so I didn’t need to do that. But I’m almost certain that camera would have assisted us.”
Mello, while saying he “didn’t want to get ahead of myself,” believes Flock cameras have “drastically reduced” stolen cars.
When he was chief in 2018 during a rash of break-ins off the Beacon Avenue exit, Mello said the thieves were driving stolen cars and, if the camera had been installed then on 138, the second they drove past that Flock site they would have been flagged.
He said thieves are “probably intelligent enough to know the likelihood” of them being reported in an area to steal cars “has risen tremendously because of that technology.”
Brine referenced more intrusive technology that already has been operating for years.
“If you’re going to be upset about this, there is live video streaming of the bridge traffic that you can check,” he said. “I’m sure it’s used for law enforcement purposes also, and it’s very useful. But that’s probably more of a privacy infraction than this, which is more specifically for law enforcement.”
Councilman Eddie Ross said if the councilors “truly don’t have any real rights” on whether the Jamestown camera remains in operation, it could be a better option to support the initiative than counter it. The collaboration between state and local police could be weakened due to a spat over the camera, he added.
Ross, however, also said he understood the concerns.
“It’s new and its novel,” he said. “While other countries use technology like Flock, we have different thoughts about privacy in this country. I think this starts to bump up against people’s comfort zone.”
summary: Dan McKee paused new installations of Flock cameras on state property Tuesday less than 12 hours after the town council discussed the controversial technology at its meeting Monday. “Automated license plate readers can be an important tool for law enforcement to solve crimes, recover stolen vehicles and locate dangerous or missing individuals, but Rhode Islanders also have legitimate questions about privacy, transparency and how this information is collected, stored and shared,” McKee said.
